# Teacher prompt


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

The teacher is a large model, Claude, that writes the message for each
synthetic triage record. Its messages are the training targets for the
SLM, so this prompt defines what a good message is. It follows the
structure of
[write_prose](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/aai-coding/blob/main/aai_coding/write_prose.py):
rules, good examples, one bad message with its mistakes marked, a
numbered list of failure modes, and plain words to use. The SLM never
sees this prompt. Fine-tuning builds the behaviour into it, so the
prompt’s length only costs the teacher, and prompt caching covers most
of that.

The failure modes are shared. The code checks in
[`checks`](02_checks.ipynb) cover some of them, and the judges and the
annotation app will use the same list for the rest, until expert error
analysis replaces it.

## Rules

The rules restate the message rules of the [scope](design/scope.ipynb)
for the teacher. The triage contract keeps them simple: items arrive
most severe first, and `since` is a phrase to copy.

The context and rules, as the teacher reads them:

``` python
Markdown(f'{CONTEXT}\n\n{RULES}')
```

You write short WhatsApp messages to coffee farmers. Each message turns
one triage record into actions. The record comes from monitoring code,
which has already decided which problems matter, how severe they are,
and what the data shows about their cause. Only some plants carry a
sensor, and each sensor stands for the plants around it.

- Write one paragraph per item, in the record’s order.
- Start each paragraph with the item’s marker (👀 early, ⚠️ moderate, 🚨
  severe), then its location exactly as written in the record, then a
  colon.
- After the colon, say in plain words what is wrong and when it started,
  then what to do. Say only what the record reports, and never name a
  cause or a part it does not report, such as a valve, a battery or a
  radio link. Never write likely, may, might or probably.
- Say when the problem started with the record’s `since` phrase, as it
  is. When `soil_water` has the same phrase, say it once, such as “have
  had no water and shown water stress for a week or more”.
- After the location, refer to it with words such as “this line”, “this
  plot” or “this plant”. Never repeat the location or part of it.
- Write no digits outside the locations: no readings, counts or dates.
  Speak of monitored plants. For a single node, say “a monitored plant”
  or “this plant”.
- Every cluster or widespread item has an
  [`amount`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/coffee.html#amount)
  word: all, almost all, most or some. Use it as it is, even when it is
  all, as in “all monitored plants on this line”.
- For water stress, `soil_water` says whether water still reaches the
  soil. When it is `none` with a phrase, say that no water has reached
  the soil since then, and point to the irrigation where the pattern
  does: whether water reaches this plant for one node, the line from its
  start to the last plant for a cluster, the irrigation schedule and the
  water supply for the whole farm.
- When `soil_water` is `arriving`, say that the soil still gets water.
  For one node or a cluster, suggest checking the plants for heat
  damage, pests or root problems. For the whole farm, the heat is the
  cause, so suggest longer or more frequent irrigation.
- For equipment faults, `fault` says what the data shows. For
  `missing data`, say that the sensors have sent no data and that the
  plants they cover are not monitored. For `implausible values`, say
  that the `sensor` gives values that look wrong. For
  `camera view changed`, say that the camera no longer sees the plant’s
  leaves.
- For faults, point to where to look: the node’s power and connection
  for one node, the power supply its nodes share for a cluster, the
  gateway and its power supply for the whole farm.
- For severe items, say that the action is for today.
- Be plain, friendly and direct. No greeting, no sign-off, no
  explanation of the monitoring.
- Keep the whole message under 600 characters.

## A bad message

This message for the first example makes most of the mistakes the
teacher must avoid. Each bracketed number refers to a failure mode in
the next section, and the last line marks the item it leaves out:

``` python
Markdown(f'```text\n{BAD}\n```')
```

``` text
Hello! [1][5] Our monitoring system has analysed your farm today. [2]

⚠️ [6] Block F, drip line F2: most [11] nodes [3] are flagged [3] for water stress since 21 July [4] because the valve is stuck [14]. Block F, drip line F2 [8] may need attention. [9] Please check your farm. [10]

Have a great day! [1]

[7: the item at Block C, drip line C3 is missing]
```

Without its markers, the bad message fails five of the code checks. The
others, such as the greeting, the jargon and the hedging, need a judge:

``` python
res = check(EXAMPLES[0]['record'], re.sub(r'\[[^\]]*\]', '', BAD))
test_eq({k for k, v in res.items() if not v}, {'format', 'coverage', 'severity', 'no_numbers', 'amount'})
res
```

    {'format': False,
     'coverage': False,
     'no_invented': True,
     'severity': False,
     'no_numbers': False,
     'length': True,
     'amount': False}

Each failure mode has a short name, what goes wrong, and the fix.
`checks` names the code checks that catch it, and is empty when a judge
must decide.

## The prompt

[`system_prompt`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/teacher.html#system_prompt)
assembles the parts in the order of write_prose: context, rules, good
examples, the bad message, the failure modes, then plain words.
[`user_prompt`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/teacher.html#user_prompt)
gives the record as JSON, and
[`prompt_version`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/teacher.html#prompt_version)
identifies the prompt:

## Writing messages

[`teach`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/teacher.html#teach)
sends the prompt and one record to the teacher through
[fastllm](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/fastllm), which also reaches
other providers and llama.cpp’s OpenAI-compatible server, so the
baseline and fine-tuned models can go through the same client later.
Each call gets a fresh chat, so records never see each other. A
temperature of 0.3 keeps the messages consistent and still varies their
wording. Haiku is the teacher, as the scope’s Choice of teacher section
explains, and `model` selects another one.

[`teach`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/teacher.html#teach)
returns the message with its provenance, as the Choice of teacher
section requires: the model, the temperature, the prompt version and the
date. The prompt version is a short hash of the system prompt, so
messages written with different prompts are never compared by mistake.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/teacher.py#L129"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### teach

``` python
async def teach(
    rec:dict, # Triage record
    model:str='claude-haiku-4-5', # Teacher model
    temp:float=0.3, # Sampling temperature
    note:str='', # Added after the record, such as the mistakes of a previous attempt
)->dict: # The message, with the model, temperature, prompt version and date that produced it
```

*Have the teacher write the message for `rec`*

<details open class="code-fold">
<summary>Exported source</summary>

``` python
MODEL, TEMP = 'claude-haiku-4-5', 0.3
```

</details>

Calling the teacher needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, which `load_dotenv` reads
from the project’s untracked `.env` file. This cell does not run in
tests:

``` python
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
rec = sample(DIMS, triage, 10, seed=3)[8]['input']
await teach(rec)
```

For this record, with an implausible air temperature reading and two
cameras whose view has changed, Haiku wrote:

> 👀 Block G, row 12: the air temperature sensor at this plant has given
> values that look wrong since today. Check that it is not damaged and
> that nothing blocks airflow around it.
>
> 👀 Block D, row 21: the camera at this plant has not seen its leaves
> since today. Check that it points at the plant and that nothing blocks
> its view.
>
> 👀 Block H, row 14: the camera at this plant has not seen its leaves
> since today. Check that it points at the plant and that nothing blocks
> its view.
